paper_title: PRISM: PRIvileged Sibling-guided Multi-Agent Topology Design

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-agent systems (MAS) based on large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful way to address complex problems, and their effectiveness depends critically on the collaboration topology that decides which agents participate and how they communicate. Recent work learns to generate this topology from the task query, fitting the generator to corpora of execution-verified graphs. The post-training method for such generators remains a limitation: a corpus lists the graphs that solved a query but never ranks them, leaving continued supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with no per-query preference to exploit. Without such a preference, the generator drifts toward the topologies the corpus contains most often rather than those that suit each query, so a gain on one task can come at a cost on another. We propose PRISM, which recovers per-query signal from the same corpus by learning with privileged information: a teacher reads, through a zero-initialized low-rank branch, a sibling graph that also solved the query and is unavailable at deployment, and the student matches its per-decision targets on trajectories the student samples itself. Across six diverse benchmarks PRISM improves over every topology-design baseline evaluated, and matched-teacher controls support the contribution of privileged query information. Code is available in this link.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Multi-agent Systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs) address complex tasks by coordinating agents with complementary roles. Their effectiveness depends on the collaboration topology: the graph specifying which agents participate and how information flows between them (Zhuge et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2025). Consequently, improving MAS requires learning how to organize collaboration alongside improving the capabilities of individual agents. Research on automated topology design has expanded from predefined workflows to learned communication structures and, more recently, generators that construct collaboration graph for each query (Li et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025b). These generators learn which agents to include and how to connect them for given query. Recent work has made query-conditioned topology generation feasible by deriving supervision from multi-agent execution outcomes (Li et al., 2026b;c). Candidate collaboration graphs are instantiated and executed on training queries, and empirically successful querygraph pairs are retained as training examples. Using these verified pairs, an autoregressive topology generator learns through teacher forcing to predict agent roles and communication links conditioned on the query and the partially constructed graph. This approach turns previous collaboration outcomes into reusable supervision and provides straightforward post-training strategy: continuing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on verified graphs. However, closer agreement with the recorded graphs does not necessarily translate into better downstream task performance. In our experiments, continued SFT concentrates the generated topology distribution, while its effects on downstream performance vary across benchmarks: some improve, whereas others exhibit limited gains or regressions. This observation is consistent with prior findings that likelihood-based SFT can reduce output diversity (Li et al., 2025), although concentration alone does not establish whether the resulting topologies are more effective. Teacher forcing also introduces mismatch between the partial graphs encountered during training and inference. Training supervises decisions 1 Preprint. Under review. along recorded construction trajectories, whereas deployment requires the generator to act on partial graphs produced by its own preceding decisions. Deviations from recorded trajectories can therefore lead to partial graphs for which the verified corpus provides no direct supervision. This mismatch parallels exposure bias in autoregressive imitation learning and motivates on-policy distillation (Lin et al., 2020; Agarwal et al., 2024): using teacher to guide construction decisions at partial graphs visited by the student. In this work, we propose PRISM, which addresses this training-inference mismatch by distilling verified-graph information at the partial graphs actually visited by the student. For each training query, the student first generates its own partial graph trajectory. privileged teacher then receives the query together with another verified graph for the same query and provides soft distribution over the next topology decisions at each student-generated partial graph. Thus, supervision remains available even after the student deviates from the recorded verified trajectory, directly addressing the off-trajectory states left unsupervised by teacher-forced SFT. The query-matched verified graph also provides information about successful alternative construction, while supervised anchoring preserves the verified graph trajectories and discourages the student from drifting away from valid topology patterns. Since the verified graphs are collected before post-training, PRISM requires no additional MAS executions, and the privileged input is removed at inference time without changing the deployed topology generator. In summary, this work makes the following contributions: We document increased output concentration under continued supervised fine-tuning of an autoregressive topology designer and relate it to accuracy across benchmarks. We propose PRISM, which uses successful sibling graphs as training-only privileged inputs for on-policy self-distillation, without additional post-training LLM executions or changes to the deployed designer architecture. We demonstrate its effect across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, general reasoning and code generation - GSM8K, MultiArith, SVAMP, AQuA, MMLU and HumanEval - outperforming the strongest topology-generation baseline on each. Matched teacher controls support an additional benefit from query-matched graph information beyond constant-input on-policy distillation.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: MAS communication topology design. Early approaches organize reasoning and collaboration through chains (Wei et al., 2022; Hong et al., 2024), tree-structured search (Yao et al., 2023), and debate protocols (Du et al., 2024). In MAS, performance depends on the communication structure (Qian et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2025), while the computational cost of collaboration has motivated research on efficiency (Li et al., 2026a). Automated topology design methods optimize agent participation and communication: AgentPrune (Zhang et al., 2025a) prunes communication edges, AgentDropout (Wang et al., 2025) removes agents and edges across communication rounds, and G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2025b) generates task-conditioned communication graphs using variational graph autoencoder. These methods operate on predefined set of candidate agents. ARGDESIGNER (Li et al., 2026b) extends the design space by autoregressively generating agent roles and communication edges, allowing the number of agents and their role composition to vary with the query. Complementary research investigates on-policy refinement using failure trajectories for agent safety alignment (Yin et al., 2026) and adversarial manipulation that increases the computational cost of tool-augmented reasoning (Li & Wang, 2026). Our work focuses on post-training an autoregressive topology generator initialized through supervised learning on execution-verified graphs. We retain ARG-DESIGNERs deployed architecture and introduce privileged teacher to provide additional supervision along student-generated graph trajectories. On-policy distillation. DAgger (Ross et al., 2011) learns from states the policy itself visits rather than states demonstrator recorded, and GKD (Agarwal et al., 2024) and MiniLLM (Gu et al., 2024) bring that idea into LLM distillation, sampling from the student and scoring with teacher; the latter also motivates mode-seeking reverse KL. further line makes teacher and student one model rather than large-small pair: Zhao et al. (2026) distil reasoner from its own on-policy samples, and Dat et al. (2026) carry the scheme to diffusion language models. PRISM uses on-policy self-distillation 2 Preprint. Under review. in this sense, separating teacher from student by privileged input rather than by scale or by an Its decision spaces are also small categorical decision spaces (roles + END; earlier checkpoint. edge/no-edge), so the divergence is exact rather than estimated.

sections.title: 4 PRISM
sections.content: PRISM provides an alternative supervision pathway for exploiting the querygraph associations already present in the verified corpus. As shown in Figure 1, Stage 1 constructs teacher conditioned on successful sibling graph, and Stage 2 distils its predictions on trajectories sampled from the students current policy.

sections.title: 4.1 STAGE 1: CONSTRUCT THE PRIVILEGED TEACHER
sections.content: Let be privileged information for query Q: information that exists at training time and is structurally unavailable at deployment. We clone the student and give the clone one extra input branch; writing fa for the encoding of a, the teachers conditioning vector is FiLM modulation (Perez et al., 2018) of the students: cteacher = TaskProc(fQ) (cid:0)1 + γ(fa)(cid:1) + β(fa), (4) where fa passes through small encoder - layer normalisation, dropout, linear map to rank = 16 and tanh activation - before γ and β are computed. Starting from pretrained ARG-Designer checkpoint θ0, the teacher minimizes the weighted supervised objective in Eq. 2, updating all teacher parameters. The student itself receives no updates and remains at θ0 throughout this stage. γ, β : Rr Rd, 3 Preprint. Under review. Figure 1: Overview of PRISM. Stage 0 fits the designer on execution-verified topologies, which also supply the privileged input a. Stage 1 trains separate teacher whose FiLM branch reads a. Stage 2 has the teacher rescore the students own trajectories, the student minimising Eq. 6. Stage 3 deploys the student alone; the teacher is discarded. Sibling sampling and encoding. Each successful graph is converted into deterministic text representation of its roles and edges, which is embedded using the same frozen MiniLM encoder (Wang et al., 2020) used for the query. Duplicate graph representations are merged before sibling sampling. For verified target graph G, the sibling is drawn uniformly from the other graphs that solved the same query, skipping any whose text representation is identical to Gs, which keeps the target itself out of the privileged channel. The sibling is resampled every epoch, allowing the pairing to change when multiple eligible candidates exist. If query has no distinct successful sibling, its privileged input is zero vector; no graph from another query is substituted. This supplies no sibling-specific graph information, although zero input does not necessarily produce an identity FiLM modulation after training. The implementation counts queries without siblings and stops training if no query has an eligible sibling. The teacher is separate model initialized from copy of the student weights θ0 and augmented with privileged encoder and FiLM branch; no parameters are shared between the models. Under identical deterministic evaluation conditions, zero initialization of the FiLM output maps makes the teachers predictions identical to the students at teacher creation. This removes an initial functional mismatch, but does not imply equal model capacity or zero divergence after teacher training. During Stage 2 the teacher is frozen and every student parameter is trainable. The channel is kept narrow because the cold start yields only O(103) graphs: at rank 16 it adds 20k parameters against 592k for full-width channel at = 384, an approximately 30-fold reduction in channel parameters while retaining competitive accuracy in the evaluated settings (7).

sections.title: 4.2 STAGE 2: ON-POLICY SELF-DISTILLATION
sections.content: At the start of Stage 2, we sample one verified reference graph uniformly from the deduplicated set of successful topologies for each training query. This reference is fixed throughout Stage 2 and shared across all rollouts for that query. Unlike the target-exclusion rule used in Stage 1, Stage 2 does not exclude references that match the supervised anchor or sampled rollout. Queries with single verified topology use that topology as their reference. Student trajectories are resampled at every optimization step. For each query we sample complete topologies from the current student policy at temperature τ , so that the corrected states are always the ones this policy visits, unlike off-policy pseudo-labelling, where graphs are generated once and reused as the student drifts away from them. Each trajectory 4 Preprint. Under review. Table 1: Pass@1/accuracy (%) on six benchmarks with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Best results are bold. Although their parameters are separate, the teacher and student predict over the same node and edge symbol sets, so every per-decision categorical divergence between them is computed exactly rather than estimated: LKL = α Enode steps (cid:1)(cid:3) + (1 α) Eedge slots (cid:2)KL(cid:0)Pθ Pteacher (cid:2)KL(cid:0)Pθ Pteacher (cid:1)(cid:3) , (5) with α = 0.2 inherited from Eq. 2. We use reverse KL to encourage concentration on decisions favored by the teacher and evaluate this choice against alternative divergences (Gu et al., 2024). To retain direct supervision from verified querygraph pairs, we combine the distillation objective with supervised anchoring loss: Lanchor = log Pθ(Greal Q), LPRISM = (1 λ) LKL + λ Lanchor (6) where Greal is verified graph for drawn from the corpus of Eq. 3. The two terms are normalised differently and we keep the convention explicit: Lanchor sums the log-probabilities of all node and edge decisions of Greal, unweighted by α, and averages over the batch, whereas each divergence in Eq. 5 is mean over decision points of its own kind. Setting λ = 1 leaves the anchor alone, which is the objective of our SFT control, making it the far endpoint of this one-parameter family rather than different method. Rollouts are scored as sampled, never repaired first: repaired graph is not what the policy emitted, and its gradient would not match the state it came from. Gradients flow only through the re-scoring of those trajectories; sampling itself is not differentiated and the teacher is evaluated without gradients, so we optimise the divergence at the visited states rather than an exact gradient of the expectation over πθ, as is standard in on-policy distillation (Agarwal et al., 2024). The teacher is frozen throughout Stage 2 and discarded before evaluation, so the deployed model is architecturally identical to ARG-DESIGNER and the privileged channel exists only during training. The full loop is Algorithm 1 in Appendix B.

sections.title: 5.1 SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks and backbone. Following Li et al. (2026b) we evaluate on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MultiArith (Roy & Roth, 2016), SVAMP (Patel et al., 2021), AQuA (Ling et al., 2017), and HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), reporting Pass@1 / accuracy. All agents run on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025) served locally, so every arm in every table is controlled re-run under one execution stack rather than number copied from paper. The role encoder is all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Wang et al., 2020) with = 384, and = 1 round with summariser. Stage 1 uses 40 epochs at lr 104; Stage 2 uses 30 epochs at 104, 16 queries per step, = 4 rollouts per query, τ = 1.0, α = 0.2, λ = 0.3 and reverse KL (Appendix A), shared across benchmarks with no per-benchmark tuning. Data source and partitioning. Our verified graph corpus uses questions from MIXCHAIN, MBPP and MMLU. The training and validation data are partitioned by query rather than by graph. Graphs are grouped by their associated query, the query groups are shuffled with fixed seed, and 20% are assigned to validation. While MIXCHAIN supplies the corpus for the four mathematical benchmarks, general reasoning and code generation are covered separately: Stage 0 builds verified corpus for MMLU from its own questions and, for code generation, from MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), 5 Preprint. HumanEval is therefore used for evaluation only, so no question it scores has contributed training graph to any arm. Baselines and controls. We compare against ARG-DESIGNER (Li et al., 2026b), G-Designer (Zhang et al., 2025b), AgentPrune (Zhang et al., 2025a) and AgentDropout (Wang et al., 2025), and single-agent vanilla run. ARG-DESIGNER is reproduced in full: the cold start of Eq. 3 followed by the published efficiency fine-tuning stage, so the row labelled ARG-DESIGNER is the complete training procedure of (Li et al., 2026b) rather than an initialization-only variant. The critical control is SFT: continued supervised maximum likelihood on the verified corpus from that same deployed checkpoint θ0, matched to Stage 2 in epochs and learning rate. Both SFT and PRISM are initialized from the deployed ARG-Designer checkpoint. Their student-training stages use 30 epochs and learning rate of 104. PRISM additionally trains teacher for 40 epochs and performs trajectory sampling and teacher rescoring during distillation. Both methods reuse the existing verified corpus without additional multi-agent executions during post-training. These settings match the student-training schedule, but not total training computation. Table 1 scores the model each procedure finally deploys. Beyond these arm-level controls, Appendix executes chosen crews directly on fixed question set, holding wiring, rounds, decision method and backbone fixed so that only the role composition varies.

sections.title: 5.2 MAIN RESULTS
sections.content: PRISM is the best method on every benchmark, but two features of Table 1 matter more than the headline. The first is the AQuA column: SFT tracks or beats the baseline on five of the six benchmarks, by at most 6.15% and never falling more than 0.10% below, then drops 12.60% on AQuA. The effect of continued SFT varies substantially across benchmarks. The second is the size of PRISMs margin over SFT, which varies by an order of magnitude across those same benchmarks: 0.72% on MMLU and 1.89% on GSM8K against 13.78% on AQuA. Cost. Table 2 reports the deployment cost of each designer. PRISM averages 3.04 agents per query against 3.00 for ARG-DESIGNER and SFT alike. At = 1 that is 4.04 LLM calls against 4.00, buying 2.56% and 3.24% more accuracy for 1.0% more calls. Post-training adds no executions either, since its rollouts sample graph trajectories rather than running any agent.

sections.title: 5.4 DIFFICULTY-MATCHED CONTROL
sections.content: On AQuA, SFT has lower accuracy on questions for which it emits its modal role assignment. We therefore partition each benchmark by whether SFT emitted its default crew and score both arms on exactly those questions, so the two face an identical set and difficulty cannot differ between them. Table 4 shows an advantage in both groups, largest on the questions where SFT emitted its modal role composition. It does not establish that the crew caused the errors, since crew composition, wiring, graph size and the stochastic execution of the agent runtime all vary together across the two designers, so what the partition isolates is the designer and not the crew. On AQuA, PRISM improves in both groups: +18.7% where SFT emitted its modal crew (79.1% against 60.4%, exact McNemar = 0.0001) and +11.0% elsewhere (p = 0.003). The margin is largest on the defaulted questions, but it is not confined to them, so the fixed crew accounts for part of the AQuA gap rather than all of it. The other benchmarks separate the groups far less: GSM8K gains about point in each (+1.1% against +2.4%, neither significant at the 5% level) and SVAMP gains 3.0% where SFT defaults against 0.3% elsewhere, neither significant. On those 91 AQuA questions PRISM emits 18 distinct topologies and repeats SFTs default crew on only one question in eight, so the crews that replace it are themselves varied.

sections.title: 6 DISCUSSION
sections.content: Two objections stand between 5.4 and our account of it: that the channel works through added parameters and training steps rather than through what it carries, and that the advantage is owed to on-policy correction any teacher would supply. We answer the first with measurements independent of downstream accuracy, the second with matched pair of Stage-2 runs.

sections.title: 6.2 CONTENT VERSUS PROCEDURE
sections.content: The above establishes that the teacher reads the channel, not that what it reads survives distillation into student that never sees it. We separate content from procedure with matched Stage 2: two students from the same initialisation, identical in rollouts, α, λ, KL direction, epochs and learning rate, differing only in which teacher supplies the target. The shuffled teacher is fully trained and simply carries no information about this query, so its student still receives on-policy correction on its own visited states - it is PRISM with the privilege removed and nothing else changed. The constant teacher separates the two effects that the PRISMSFT gap confounds, and shows that the shuffled teacher is not clean null: the constant arm beats it on all six benchmarks (83.86 against 82.58 on average), so conditioning on another querys graph misleads the student rather than merely withholding information. PRISM still exceeds the constant teacher on all six (+1.66% on average, sign test = 0.031) at matched teacher epochs, sampling, supervision, loss mixture and computation, which leaves privileged content as the remaining difference. AQuA carries both contributions, from SFT at 62.60 to the constant teacher at 71.65 (+9.05% from on-policy distillation) and PRISM at 76.38 (+4.73% from content), and distillation alone is not sufficient: the constant teacher improves on SFT on three benchmarks only, losing 1.11% on MMLU.

sections.title: 7.2 KL DIRECTION
sections.content: Figure 5 varies the divergence with the channel fixed to sibling graph: reverse is KL(PθPteacher), forward KL reverses the arguments, and JSD their mixture at β = 0.5. Reverse KL achieves the highest average score among the evaluated divergence objectives (85.52 against 84.85 and 83.90) and on every mathematical benchmark; forward KL achieves slightly higher accuracy on HumanEval and MMLU by 0.61% and 0.33%, gaps small enough that we do not infer mechanistic explanation from these small differences. The margin is widest on GSM8K and SVAMP, where reverse KL leads forward KL by 1.89% and 2.10% and JSD by 2.80% and 3.00%. This is the pattern the mode-seeking argument predicts: with several verified graphs per query, mass-covering objective spreads the student across the teachers modes, reproducing the averaging that limits SFT, whereas reverse KL commits it to one.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced PRISM, method for post-training autoregressive multi-agent topology generators using successful sibling graphs as privileged inputs. The teacher provides decision-level targets on student-generated trajectories, and the deployed student uses only the query. Under the evaluated Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct configuration, PRISM improves mean accuracy over ARG-Designer across six benchmarks with similar average number of agent calls. constant-input teacher control indicates that sibling information contributes beyond the matched distillation procedure. The results do not establish that PRISM recovers ranking among successful graphs or that query-specific crew assignment explains the gains. Future evaluation should test that assignment effect on representative held-out questions, compare post-training methods at matched compute, and examine transfer across different backbones. 9 Preprint. Under review.

Repairs are applied at evaluation only, never to sampled graph before scoring. Four edits make sampled graph executable. First, during evaluation-time generation, any node after the first whose edge head emitted no incoming edge receives one at uniformly random admissible position, which guarantees V 1. The generated graph is then made acyclic by deleting one edge from each directed cycle, any disconnected component is joined to the largest by single edge oriented from the lower to the higher node index, and any node still isolated is linked to uniformly random other node. 13 Preprint. sections.title: D SEED VARIABILITY
sections.content: Every arm is post-trained three times from the same deployed checkpoint θ0 under seeds 42, 43 and 44, the runs differing in nothing else, and each run is evaluated on the full benchmark suite. Table 8 reports the mean and sample standard deviation over the three runs; seed 42 is the run reported in Table 1 and everywhere else in the paper. 14 Preprint. Under review. Table 8: Accuracy over three post-training runs per arm, under seeds 42, 43 and 44. Each cell is the mean, with the sample standard deviation over the three runs as subscript. Arm GSM8K MultiArith SVAMP AQuA HumanEval MMLU ARG-DESIGNER SFT constant teacher PRISM 72.280.64 80.210.75 73.090.54 86.180.09 86.710.04 73.291.02 87.770.57 98.890.26 93.470.47 76.511.38 82.520.35 73.760.55 98.330.50 98.830.00 98.660.29 79.070.35 80.290.35 81.510.35 75.331.38 62.730.61 69.421.94 92.930.51 92.730.42 92.370.29 Run-to-run spread is small beside the differences the paper reports. The largest standard deviation on any benchmark is 1.94, on AQuA, where the three arms conditioned on the query alone are least stable, and most lie below 0.6, while the benchmark-averaged accuracy varies by at most 0.20 within an arm. Against that, PRISM leads SFT by 3.18 on the benchmark average, an order of magnitude larger than either arms spread. The per-benchmark picture is the one the main text describes, with one qualification. Treating the seeds as paired runs, PRISM exceeds SFT in all three on GSM8K, SVAMP, AQuA, HumanEval and MMLU; on MultiArith the two are indistinguishable (98.89 against 98.83, paired difference +0.06 0.26, with PRISM ahead in one seed, level in one and behind in one), so the 0.34% margin visible in Table 1 is seed noise rather than an effect, and MultiArith is better read as saturated. PRISM exceeds ARG-DESIGNER on the mean of every benchmark, including MultiArith (+0.56) and AQuA (+1.18), and does so in all three seeds. Two properties of SFT also reproduce. Its AQuA accuracy remains near 63% across the evaluated seeds while ARG-DESIGNER stays near 75, so the uneven transfer documented in 5.3 is property of the training configuration and not an unlucky run. And SFTs benchmark average, 82.310.10, sits below the checkpoint it starts from, 83.030.17: continued supervised fine-tuning on the verified corpus buys large gains on GSM8K and HumanEval and pays for them elsewhere, which is the pattern PRISM is designed to avoid.

The sizes differ substantially: the excess of I(Q; G) over each arms null is 0.017 nats for the cold start, 0.051 for SFT and 0.160 for PRISM, which is 1.1%, 2.0% and 5.8% of each arms output entropy, and the bootstrap intervals for SFT and PRISM do not overlap. Most of the raw plug-in statistic is estimator bias at eight samples per query, which is why the excess rather than the raw value is the comparable quantity. The deployed ARG-DESIGNER checkpoint is the most query-conditional arm measured (excess 0.377 nats over its own null) while being the least accurate of the three deployed designers in Table 1. Greater measured query dependence therefore does not necessarily correspond to higher downstream accuracy. These diagnostics show that the generated graph distributions depend on the query; they do not establish that this dependence accounts for the accuracy improvement.

sections.content: The controls of 5.4 compare designers, so topology and the designer that produced it vary together. We therefore execute chosen crews directly. The question set is the 91 AQuA questions on which 16 Preprint. Under review. SFT emitted its modal crew the SFT emitted default group of Table 4. Every condition supplies only role multiset; wiring is chain in all conditions, with one round, the same decision method and the same backbone, and each condition is executed three times. SFTs own crew and its modal crew in canonical order share role multiset by construction and differ only in the order of roles along the chain. Comparison p(vote) per run modal crew vs PRISM 7 SFTs crew vs PRISM 4 modal crew vs random 2 6 PRISM vs random 9 PRISM vs permuted 4 permuted vs random 0.0002 0.0009 30 21 28 < 0.0001 9 9 7 0.6072 1.0000 0.5488 0.002, 0.001, 0.000 0.087, 0.036, 0.000 0.003, 0.001, 0.000 1.000, 1.000, 0.118 0.832, 0.832, 0.804 1.000, 0.839, 0.302 Executing SFTs own crew reaches 61.54% against PRISMs 77.66% on the same questions, difference of 4 against 21 paired disagreements (exact McNemar = 0.0009). With the designers removed from the comparison and wiring, rounds, decision method and backbone held fixed, the crew is what differs, so this is causal evidence at the level of topology rather than the association of 5.4. Two further conditions bound how much this supports. size-matched random crew reaches 75.46% and is not distinguishable from PRISMs crews (6 against 9, = 0.61), and we detect no statistically significant difference between the original and permuted crew assignments on this subset (9 against 9, = 1.00). The supported conclusion is therefore narrow: SFTs modal crew is worse than the alternatives on these questions, and both the random-crew and permuted-crew controls recover much of the observed performance gap. This intervention does not establish that PRISMs particular crews, or their assignment to particular queries, carry benefit beyond that. We note that the question set is selected by SFTs behaviour, which works against detecting matching effect, so the permutation result is failure to detect rather than evidence of absence. Composition is also not the whole story. Forcing the modal crew in canonical order scores 53.85% against 61.54% for the same multiset in the order SFT emitted, difference larger than any percondition spread in Table 11, so role order along the chain matters at fixed composition and the crew abstraction used throughout 5.3 is not order-invariant.
